title: Financial Theft
summary: Financial theft covers adversary activity whose purpose is to take money, whether by direct transfer, fraud, extortion, or manipulation of cryptocurrency systems. It is rarely a single technique; it is a goal reached through chains such as compromising an account and impersonating a trusted party to authorise a payment, or encrypting and exfiltrating data and then demanding payment to restore access and prevent publication. The distinguishing feature for defenders is that impact is measured in currency rather than in downtime alone, and that the victim set often includes third parties such as customers, suppliers, and payment providers. Telemetry is scattered across mail security, identity providers, finance systems, and endpoint logs, because the social engineering, the account compromise, and the transfer happen in different places. Investigations therefore focus on mailbox rules and forwarding, sign-in anomalies, changes to payment details, and the interval between the intrusion and the fraudulent transaction.

beginner.definition: Financial theft means attackers taking money rather than only data. They may trick a person into paying a fake invoice, or take over an account and send funds. Sometimes they hold files hostage and demand payment. The aim is money in their own pocket.
beginner.whyItMatters: Money lost this way is often gone for good, unlike data that can be restored from a backup. A single fraudulent transfer can cost more than the whole security programme. It also damages trust, because customers and partners are sometimes the ones who pay. Attackers know that staff under time pressure are easy to trick, so your processes matter as much as your technology.
howItWorks: The attacker studies the organisation to find out who can approve payments.
They compromise a mailbox or an account, often using a convincing fake login page.
They add hidden mail rules so replies from the real person are quietly moved aside.
They pretend to be a supplier or a manager and ask urgently for a payment.
The money leaves the account and is moved onward quickly, so it cannot be recalled.
Some attackers instead encrypt files and demand payment before they will restore them.
beginner.example: Picture a busy market where each stall pays its supplier at the end of the week. One morning a stallholder receives a neat letter that looks exactly like the usual invoice. It even carries the right logo. The only change is the bank account number at the bottom, with a note asking for payment today. The stallholder is rushed and pays it. The money lands in a stranger's account and is moved on within minutes, while the real supplier is still waiting. Financial theft in computers follows the same pattern. The attacker does not break the till open; they change one detail and let the normal process do the work.
takeaways: Verify any change of payment details by calling a known number, never one from the message.
Check mailbox rules and forwarding after any suspected account compromise.
Treat urgency and secrecy in a payment request as a warning sign.

objectives: Explain what financial theft means as an attacker goal rather than a single technique.
Describe how business email compromise leads to an unauthorised transfer.
Identify the mailbox and identity signals that come before a fraudulent payment.
Explain how ransomware extortion turns access into a payment demand.
Outline the checks that prevent a payment redirection.
